notable_claims: The NCSA email policy prohibits e-mail that 'attempts to disadvantage NCSA'.
The policy allows for the search of mbox files without user permission or suspicion.
Institutional ownership of computer facilities does not override constitutional protections against unreasonable search and seizure.
classification.summary: Carl Kadie criticizes a new email policy at the National Center for Supercomputer Applications (NCSA) that allows searches and punishment for users who 'attack' the University or NCSA. Kadie argues the policy is overly broad, lacks due process, and violates First and Fourth Amendment rights as well as established academic freedom principles. He specifically challenges the notion that institutional ownership of computer facilities justifies the suspension of privacy and free expression.
classification.title: New NCSA e-mail policy inconsistent with Academic Freedom

identity.subject: New NCSA e-mail policy inconsistent with Academic Freedom

notable_claims: NCSA implemented a policy on April 1st permitting searches of mboxes to prevent users from disadvantaging the organization.
An employee was fired after being identified as the sender of anonymous emails.
classification.summary: A report regarding a new email policy at the National Center for Supercomputing Applications (NCSA) following an incident involving anonymous emails. The policy reportedly allows the organization to search users' mailboxes if they are suspected of using email to disadvantage the NCSA. This occurred after a student employee was identified and fired for sending 'rude' messages.
classification.title: New NCSA e-mail policy inconsistent with Academic Freedom
